## Mark 5:1–22 — Research notes

**v. 1 (the place)**
- The manuscripts vary between three names: Gadarenes, Gergesenes and Gerasenes. Ellicott says the better manuscripts have "Gerasenes." The Pulpit Commentary says that reading is now generally accepted and links it to a lakeside Gerasa/Kersa, not the better-known Gerasa further inland. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-1.htm
- Gill thinks the names refer to one district, named after different towns in it (Gadara, Gergesa). Benson says the same. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-1.htm
- Constable places the event on the south-east shore, near both a small village called Gergesa and the larger town of Gadara. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-1.html
- The Light of Israel commentary notes that Gerasa (modern Jerash) lies more than 30 miles from the lake. It also reports that Origen and Eusebius linked the miracle to a lakeside Gergesa. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-1.html
- The Fourfold Gospel thinks "Gerasenes" is probably a copyist's error for "Gergesenes," which is what Origen suggested. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tfg/mark-5.html
- Precept Austin quotes a "problem/solution" note that blames the differences on copyists, so there is no contradiction in the originals. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-5-commentary
- On bible.org, Ralph Earle sees no grounds for calling this a contradiction. F. F. Bruce sets out which name each Gospel uses. https://bible.org/seriespage/9-gerasene-demoniac-mark-51-20
- The Berean Study Bible notes on biblehub say this is largely Gentile Decapolis country. Jesus' deliberate crossing there points ahead to the gospel going to the nations. https://biblehub.com/mark/5-1.htm
- Poole cites Lightfoot: the large pig herds suggest the people were pagans or Jews who had abandoned their faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-1.htm
- Bridgeway also describes the people as mainly Gentiles. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-1.html
- Bible.org suggests the boat may have landed late in the evening, after the storm. That would have made the scene eerie for disciples who were already shaken. https://bible.org/seriespage/9-gerasene-demoniac-mark-51-20

**v. 2 (the man meets Jesus)**
- Benson says Matthew mentions two men. Mark probably singles out the fiercer, better-known one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-1.htm
- Haydock (Catholic) gives Augustine's explanation: Mark and Luke name only the one who was better known and more feared locally. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/mark-5.html
- Constable says the same: Mark and Luke mention only the more prominent of the two. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-5.html
- Haydock also passes on Bede's reading: the man stands for the Gentiles later converted by the apostles. The legion stands for their countless vices. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/mark-5.html
- Kretzmann (Lutheran) says the devil makes anyone under his control spiritually "unclean." Here the man's whole person, body, mind and soul, was possessed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/mark-5.html

**v. 3 (living in the tombs)**
- Guzik (Enduring Word): living among the dead and decaying went against Jewish law and human instinct. Luke adds that he wore no clothes and lived like a wild animal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/
- JFB: the tombs were cut into the rocky caves and served as shelters and hiding places. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-3.htm
- Gill notes that Jewish writers listed living in tombs as one sign of a madman. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-3.htm
- Ellicott: the better manuscripts read "no man could any longer bind him." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-3.htm
- Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary reads the man as a picture of open, wilful sinners. The law's commands are the chains, and such sinners break them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-3.htm
- MacLaren: the tombs fit him, because whatever belongs to death and corruption suits the servants of evil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-1.htm

**v. 4 (chains broken)**
- Gill: his strength could not have been his own; it came from the possession. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wes/mark/5-3.html
- Barnes: his illness had increased his strength. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wes/mark/5-3.html
- MacLaren: he had met only harsh attempts to "tame" him by force, as if he were an animal, and no gentle efforts to win him back. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-1.htm
- Constable: Mark stresses strength that kept growing, apparently as the demons' grip tightened. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-5.html
- Schaff: people tried to restrain him because he was a danger to travellers (compare Matthew 8:28). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/schaff/mark-5.html — *the search returned this commentary under a slightly different address: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/scn/mark-5.html*

**v. 5 (crying out and cutting himself)**
- JFB: frightening as he was to others, he himself suffered terribly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-5.htm
- Matthew Henry: the devil is a cruel master. He compares the cutting to Baal's prophets in 1 Kings 18. He also suggests it may have been only cuts to his bare feet from sharp stones. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_005.cfm
- Clarke (Wesleyan/Methodist): this shows what Satan *could* do to everyone if God allowed it. Yet the devil himself is on a chain. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-5.html
- Barnes: these are signs of madness, and Mark says the cause was an unclean spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-5.htm
- Gill turns it into a picture of the unconverted, who wound themselves with their own sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-5.htm
- Precept Austin, quoting Hiebert: the Greek tenses show the screaming and slashing were constant. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-5-commentary
- Bible.org (Utley): this may echo self-destruction or pagan worship practices (1 Kings 18:28). https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-5

**v. 6 (he ran and knelt)** — *one real disagreement: who was worshipping, the man or the demons?*
- **The demons, under compulsion:**
  - Calvin (Reformed) says they worshipped reluctantly. Their confession was forced, not chosen. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-6.html
  - JFB: he was not drawn willingly but driven to the Judge to hear his sentence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-6.htm
  - Pulpit: fear forced the reverence, as when "the devils also believe and shudder" (James 2:19). https://biblehub.com/mark/5-6.htm
  - Precept Austin: in the end it was the demon, not the man, doing homage. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-5-commentary
- **The man himself:**
  - Spurgeon (Baptist) argues that for a moment the man, not the devil, won out. In a sermon he uses the man as a picture of a sinner "afar off" running to Christ. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/he-ran-and-he-ran
  - Gill allows both readings and applies the verse to an awakened sinner. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-6.htm
  - Bengel: a small foretaste of Christ's lordship, since the man ran despite the demons. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-6.htm
  - Coffman: the possession split his personality, so you can't always tell what the man did from what the demon did. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-6.html
- **Other points:**
  - Matthew Henry: he used to rush *at* people in rage but ran *to* Christ in reverence. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_005.cfm
  - Pulpit: vv. 3–5 are an aside. From high ground he may have watched the boat, and even the storm being calmed. https://biblehub.com/mark/5-6.htm
  - Ellicott: he bowed with his forehead to the ground. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-6.htm

**v. 7 ("Son of the Most High God… do not torture me")**
- JFB: the tormentor dreads torment. The demons know the time of judgment is fixed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-7.htm
- Precept Austin points out the same irony. It cites a Greek lexicon (BDAG): putting Jesus "under oath" was an attempt to take away his power. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-5-commentary
- Guzik quotes a scholar: the full title was a bid to gain control over Jesus, based on the belief of the time that knowing a name gave power. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Mar/Mar_5.cfm
- Pulpit: by now the evil spirits widely believed Jesus was the Messiah. The torment they dreaded was what would follow being cast out (Luke's "abyss"). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-7.htm
- Gill: "Most High" was a title for God known even to neighbouring Gentile peoples. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-5.html
- Coffman: the plea assumes God has already promised a set time for defeating the demons. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-7.html
- Bible.org: they knew judgment was coming (Matthew 25:41; Revelation 20:10). https://bible.org/book/export/html/19341

**v. 8 ("Come out of this man")**
- Calvin: the order of events is that Jesus gave the command first, and only then did the spirits protest. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-6.html
- Ellicott: Jesus at first speaks to a single spirit. Only the reply reveals "Legion." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-8.html

**v. 9 ("Legion")**
- **Why Jesus asked the name:**
  - Guzik: so that *we* would know how serious it was. Jesus was not playing along with the old belief about name-magic. "Legion" was meant to intimidate. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-5/
  - Got Questions: the question exposed what the demons really were and showed Jesus' authority. It was not something he needed in order to drive them out. https://www.gotquestions.org/my-name-is-Legion.html
  - Constable and Fortner: he asked for the disciples' benefit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-9.html
  - Schaff: the question was probably addressed to the man, but a leading demon answered. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/scn/mark-5.html
- **What "Legion" means:**
  - Calvin: simply "a great multitude," showing how great Christ's grace is. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-9.html
  - Matthew Henry: demons are military, numerous, united, powerful and organised in ranks. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_005.cfm
  - Benson: one commander speaking for them all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-1.htm
  - Kretzmann: a disciplined army; Christians are less alert than the devil is. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/mark-5.html
  - Haydock (Catholic), citing Witham: spirits have no names except in human language. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/mark-5.html
- **A non-traditional reading:**
  - Barclay suggests a psychological cause: the man may have seen Roman legions commit atrocities. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-9.html
  - Heaster's Christadelphian commentary goes further. It treats "Legion" as the man's *belief* about himself, read against the Roman occupation, and cites claims linking the pigs to the emblem of the Tenth Legion. This is outside the traditional reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-9.html

**v. 10 (not out of the region)**
- Poole: probably because it was a pagan, ignorant place where the devil does best. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-1.htm
- Precept Austin: they had been "successful" there. It thinks this is less likely to match Luke's "abyss." https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-5-commentary
- Meyer: Mark and Luke record different traditions here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-1.htm
- MacLaren: some take it as a sign that possession was limited to the time of Christ's earthly ministry, but he doesn't think the evidence is strong enough to be sure. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-1.htm
- Precept Austin: "he" (singular) begs for "them" (plural), which supports the idea of one spokesman. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-5-commentary

**vv. 11–12 (the pigs)**
- Matthew Henry: the demons hoped that by destroying the pigs they could harm the souls of the whole region. They didn't ask to enter another person, knowing Christ would refuse. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-8.html
- He adds that the spirits went into animals unclean under the Law, a fitting place for them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-1.html

**v. 13 (the herd drowns)**
- Matthew Henry: the man only cut himself because God set a limit, as in Job ("only spare his life"). Without that limit he too would have drowned. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_005.cfm
- Fortner: Christ allowed it for his own purposes, like Satan's permission to test Job. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-9.html
- **Did Jesus have the right to destroy property?**
  - MacLaren raises the question. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-1.htm
  - The Fourfold Gospel answers that the demons did it. The owners had no more grounds to complain than if disease or flood had killed the herd. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tfg/mark-5.html
  - Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary sees mercy even in losing property while lives are spared. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-5.htm
- Haydock notes that, apart from this and the withered fig tree, all Christ's miracles were acts of kindness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/mark-5.html
- How many demons? Got Questions and Precept Austin: Scripture gives no number, though about 2,000 pigs hints at the size. https://www.gotquestions.org/my-name-is-Legion.html
- Gill: the pigs drowned in the lake; the devils did not choke them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-5.html

**v. 14 (people come to see)**
- Gill: townspeople and country folk went out to check the herdsmen's story for themselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-5.html

**v. 15 (clothed and in his right mind)**
- Barnes: he was well known, so the sudden calm proved God's power. Their fear was awe, a sense that God was present. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/erv/mark/5-6.html
- Schaff: they recognised the former terror of the district, which underlines that the possession was real. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/scn/mark-5.html
- Precept Austin (with Wuest): "right mind" means self-control as well as sanity. It is ironic that they feared the sane man as much as the madman. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-5-commentary
- Guzik (via Enduring Word) and Precept Austin preach it as a picture of what Jesus does: he changes and clothes the one he saves. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-5-commentary

**v. 17 (they beg Jesus to leave)**
- MacLaren: they would rather have their pigs than their Saviour. He calls the request fear and selfishness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-1.htm
- JFB: it wasn't only the owners. Luke says the whole district asked, so the evil spirits got what they wanted. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Mar/Mar_005.cfm
- The Geneva Study Bible notes: many admire Christ but won't give up even the least thing for him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-1.htm
- Haydock (Catholic), citing Theophylact: they were amazed but annoyed at losing their herds. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/mark-5.html
- Kretzmann: the devil's hold on the heart is subtler and worse than his hold on the body. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/mark-5.html
- The unabridged JFB warns that Christ may still take people at their word when they send him away. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/mark-5.html

**v. 18 (begs to go with him)**
- Gill: the man followed Jesus to the shore and pleaded to stay with him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-5.html

**v. 19 ("Go home… tell them")**
- Barnes lists possible reasons:
  - to leave a witness among the people;
  - to show the cure would last even with Jesus absent;
  - most likely, so as not to delay his family's joy.

  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/erv/mark/5-6.html
- MacLaren: Jesus ordered silence or speech depending on what each person needed. For this man, telling his story among people who knew him would protect him from relapse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-1.htm

**v. 20 (preaching in the Decapolis)**
- Precept Austin: it shows zeal. Told to go home, he went through ten towns, a challenge to long-time Christians. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-5-commentary
- Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary: everyone marvelled, but few followed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/5-5.htm
- Bible.org: Mark uses the whole episode to prove Jesus is the Son of God and no servant of Satan. https://bible.org/seriespage/9-gerasene-demoniac-mark-51-20

**v. 21 (back across the lake)**
- The unabridged JFB: back to the west side, at Capernaum. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/mark-5.html

**v. 22 (Jairus falls at his feet)**
- Matthew Henry: even though he was a ruler, Jairus came humbly, honouring Jesus as greater than he looked. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_005.cfm
- Barclay: Jairus had to set aside his dignity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/5-5.html
- Precept Austin: this was surprising, given how much synagogue leaders dealt with Pharisees who hated Jesus. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-5-commentary

---

**On your question 2 (Protestant differences):** I found no real split between denominations in these sources. The writers from different traditions agree on the main points:
- the possession was real;
- Christ has authority over the demons;
- the townspeople were wrong to send him away.

The differences are in interpretation and emphasis, and they cut across traditions:
- **v. 6:** whether the man or the demons did the worshipping. Calvin and JFB say the demons; Spurgeon says the man.
- **Allegory:** Gill, Fortner, Spurgeon and Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary read the man as a picture of the unconverted. Calvin and Barnes stick to the plain events.
- **Wider scheme:** Fortner's comment on v. 13 fits the event into God's purposes for his elect.

If your limits reset, the gaps worth filling are the NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, the Catholic and Orthodox sites, and the Pentecostal/charismatic sites (Sam Storms, Pneuma Review, AG) on deliverance. The Pentecostal sites are where any denominational differences would most likely show up.
